name: Nariai Universe
description: A vacuum solution with a positive cosmological constant, geometrically the product of a two dimensional de Sitter space and a sphere of the same radius (dS₂ × S²). It is the limit of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole as its horizon meets the cosmological horizon, the largest black hole a de Sitter universe can hold.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The single parameter is the cosmological constant $\Lambda$, positive and an inverse length squared, and $1/\sqrt{\Lambda}$ is the radius of both factors of the product. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Edward Kasner asked which manifolds of four dimensions satisfy the field equations with a cosmological constant when their metric splits into two independent forms of two variables each, and showed, in results he presented in 1921 and published in 1925, with a metric of positive signature, that both forms must have the same constant curvature, so that the manifold is the product of two equal spheres [kasner1925]. He embedded it in flat space of six dimensions as the intersection of two cylinders built on unit spheres, and called it "the simplest solution beyond the hypersphere" of Willem de Sitter [kasner1925]. A split into forms of three variables and one, or of two, one and one, gives no other solution, so every such manifold whose metric separates is flat or this product [kasner1925].¶Among the static, spherically symmetric solutions of Einstein's equations that Hidekazu Nariai collected in 1950 was the Lorentzian form of this product, and he worked out its properties in 1951 [nariai1950, nariai1951, krasinski1999]. Every sphere of symmetry in it has the radius $1/\sqrt{\Lambda}$, and the other two dimensions form a de Sitter space of two dimensions with that same radius [ortaggio2002]. Its Euclidean section is Kasner's product of two round spheres [bousso1996, kasner1925]. In flat space of six dimensions with one timelike direction it is the intersection of $-Z_0^2 + Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 = 1/\Lambda$ with $Z_3^2 + Z_4^2 + Z_5^2 = 1/\Lambda$, homogeneous under the group $SO(2,1) \times SO(3)$, and of Petrov type D, with $\Psi_2 = -\Lambda/3$ its one nonzero Weyl scalar [ortaggio2002]. Bruno Bertotti's uniform electromagnetic field of 1959 has the same product structure, with two curvatures that differ by an amount proportional to the field [bertotti1959, krasinski1999].¶The area of the spheres is the same everywhere, so it cannot serve as a radial coordinate, and the usual derivation of Birkhoff's theorem, which takes it as one, misses the solution [krasinski1999]. The error lies in the step that sets the area of each sphere to $4\pi r^2$, which is possible only where the gradient of the area is spacelike, as Andrzej Krasiński pointed out in 1999 [krasinski1999]. That step leaves out a timelike gradient, a null one, and a vanishing one, and with a cosmological constant and no matter a vanishing gradient admits Nariai's solution alone [krasinski1999]. Krasiński and Jerzy Plebański had proved in 1980 that every spherically symmetric vacuum solution with a cosmological constant reduces to the Schwarzschild-de Sitter metric or to Nariai's, so Nariai's solution is the exception to the usual statement of Birkhoff's theorem [krasinski1980, krasinski1999].¶Paul Ginsparg and Malcolm Perry showed in 1983, with the Euclidean formulation of quantum gravity, that de Sitter space is unstable to the nucleation of black holes [ginsparg1983]. They generated Nariai's solution from the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole by a limit in which its horizon approaches the cosmological horizon, writing the mass parameter $\mu$ as $9\mu^2\Lambda = 1 - 3\epsilon^2$ and letting $\epsilon \to 0$ [ginsparg1983, dias2003, bousso1998]. The black hole of the limit, $9\mu^2\Lambda = 1$, is the largest a de Sitter universe can hold [bousso1996, bousso1998]. Its Euclidean section is the instanton for the pair creation of black holes during inflation, the only regular one among the Euclidean Schwarzschild-de Sitter solutions, and with it Raphael Bousso and Stephen Hawking found in 1996 the rate of pair creation, relative to the nucleation of a de Sitter universe without black holes, to be $\exp(-\pi/\Lambda)$ in Planck units [bousso1996]. The black hole and cosmological horizons of the Nariai solution have the same radius and the same surface gravity, so they radiate at the same rate and stay in thermal equilibrium, at the temperature $\sqrt{\Lambda}/2\pi$ in natural units [bousso1996, ortaggio2002]. With quantum effects taken into account, Bousso and Hawking found that "most black holes evaporate before the end of inflation" [bousso1996].¶With the quantum radiation included at one loop, nearly maximal Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes "anti-evaporate", as Bousso and Hawking found in 1998 [bousso1998]. A different mode of perturbation makes them evaporate, and they showed that this mode is always excited when a pair of such black holes nucleates [bousso1998]. In the higher modes of perturbation, which Bousso studied the same year, the size of the spheres rises and falls $n$ times around the circle of the de Sitter factor [bousso1998proliferation]. Several black hole horizons then form on the Nariai solution, "a degenerate unstable handle attached to de Sitter space", and as the black holes evaporate they split space into several parts, so that de Sitter space "disintegrates into an infinite number of copies of itself" [bousso1998proliferation].¶Marcello Ortaggio found in 2002 exact impulsive gravitational waves travelling through the Nariai universe, whose wave front is a pair of spheres that never expand [ortaggio2002]. The limit of Ginsparg and Perry, taken for a pair of accelerating black holes, turns the C-metric with a cosmological constant into its counterpart of the Nariai solution, which Óscar Dias and José Lemos built in 2003 [dias2003]. With Vitor Cardoso they found in 2004 every solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations in more than three dimensions that is the product of two manifolds of constant curvature, the Nariai solution of each dimension among them [cardoso2004].

related.text: Nariai's solution is the limit $\Lambda r_s^2 \to 4/9$ of Schwarzschild-de Sitter, where its two horizons meet: the largest black hole de Sitter space can hold [ginsparg1983].

Nariai's time and radial directions form a de Sitter space of two dimensions with radius $1/\sqrt{\Lambda}$ [ortaggio2002]. Edward Kasner called the solution "the simplest solution beyond the hypersphere" of de Sitter [kasner1925].

The same kind of product, anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions and a sphere, filled with a uniform electromagnetic field. In Bruno Bertotti's solution of 1959 the two curvatures differ by an amount proportional to the field [bertotti1959, krasinski1999].

The charged black hole in de Sitter space. Take away its charge and let its black hole horizon close on the cosmological one, and in the limit the region between them is Nariai's solution [romans1992].

Edward Kasner's vacuum of 1921, which expands along some axes and contracts along another. The same year he presented the product of two equal spheres as a solution with a cosmological constant, the positive signature form of Nariai's metric [kasner1921, kasner1925].
Nariai's universe has rays that neither expand nor twist, so it sits in Kundt's class beside his waves [podolskybelan2004].

The other products of two surfaces of constant curvature. Anti-Nariai trades de Sitter space for anti-de Sitter space and the sphere for a hyperbolic plane, and Plebański and Hacyan's two have one flat factor and a uniform electromagnetic field [ortaggio2002direct].

Dust whose spheres all share one radius at each moment, the solution Ruban set beside Nariai's in 1969: both are left out when the radius of the spheres is taken to change from shell to shell [ruban1969, krasinski2001ruban].

coordinates.name: Static

parameters.description: Cosmological constant, positive and an inverse length squared; the two horizons sit at $r = \pm 1/\sqrt{\Lambda}$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length along the two dimensional de Sitter factor. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Global

parameters.description: Cosmological constant, positive and an inverse length squared; the circle of $\chi$ has its least radius, $1/\sqrt{\Lambda}$, at $t = 0$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\chi$ an angle around the circle of the de Sitter factor. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Conformal

parameters.description: Cosmological constant, positive and an inverse length squared; the future and past infinities lie at $\eta = \pm\pi/2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\eta, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, all dimensionless, with the conformal time $\eta$ related to the global chart by $\tan\eta = \sinh(\sqrt{\Lambda}\,ct)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
